comment.value:
Dear Reviewers,

As we approach the conclusion of the discussion phase, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to all reviewers for your time, thoughtful feedback, and insightful questions. We greatly appreciate your engagement in the discussion, and for indicating that our clarifications have addressed your concerns. The positive updates to your scores and evaluations are truly appreciated.

If any further questions arise or if additional clarifications would be helpful, we are fully available and happy to respond promptly.

For reviewers who have not yet had the chance to participate in the discussion, we would greatly appreciate any feedback you may be able to provide. Your perspective is important for a comprehensive assessment of the work and would meaningfully contribute to strengthening the paper.

To briefly reiterate, our submission **ThinKV**:

1. **Identifies, for the first time, that degrees of attention sparsity naturally enable dynamic thought decomposition** in reasoning models.  
2. **Introduces a hybrid, thought-adaptive quantization–eviction framework** that assigns precision and performs eviction based on thought importance and the progression of the chain of thought.  
3. **Proposes Continuous Thinking (integrated in vLLM)**, enabling efficient in-place reuse of KV memory without costly gather-based compaction—eliminating a major system bottleneck in prior approaches.

We believe these contributions will help guide future research in LRMs and beyond, while enabling practical performance improvements in real-world frameworks.

Thank you again for your time and effort in reviewing our paper.

Best regards,  
Authors of` ''ThinKV''
I appreciate the authors' response, which address my questions. I would keep my score.

## **Q2: QAQ-like quantization-sensitivity analysis across various thought types**

Thank you for sharing the reference to the QAQ paper. Following your suggestion, we have conducted a QAQ-style  KV quantization-sensitivity analysis across the three thought types identified in our work—Reasoning, Execution, and Transition. Specifically, for simplicity, we conduct this analysis using uniform INT quantization. When sweeping the precision of K or V within a given thought type, all remaining KV-cache elements of all thought types are held fixed at 8-bit, ensuring that the observed accuracy changes stem solely from the targeted quantization setting. In Tables B–D below, we independently sweep the K and V precisions from 1 to 8 bits for each thought type and report the corresponding accuracy trends for R1-Llama-70B on LiveCodeBench. We also present the above results as a plot in Appendix E.9 of the revised manuscript.

**Table B:** Quantization Sensitivity for Reasoning Thoughts
| **K Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** | **V Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** |
|----------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 1              | 0                | 1                | 0                |
| 2              | 0                | 2                | 11.5             |
| 3              | 27.3             | 3                | 38.5             |
| 4              | 51.6             | 4                | 52.94            |
| 5              | 52.94            | 5                | 52.94            |
| 6              | 52.94            | 6                | 52.94            |
| 7              | 52.94            | 7                | 52.94            |
| 8              | 52.94            | 8                | 52.94            |

**Table C:** Quantization Sensitivity for Execution Thoughts
| **K Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** | **V Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** |
|----------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 1              | 0                | 1                | 0                |
| 2              | 21.5             | 2                | 27.6             |
| 3              | 39.6             | 3                | 48.5             |
| 4              | 52.94            | 4                | 52.94            |
| 5              | 52.94            | 5                | 52.94            |
| 6              | 52.94            | 6                | 52.94            |
| 7              | 52.94            | 7                | 52.94            |
| 8              | 52.94            | 8                | 52.94            |

**Table D:** Quantization Sensitivity for Transition Thoughts
| **K Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** | **V Precision** | **Accuracy (\%)** |
|----------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 1              | 10.5             | 1                | 11.9             |
| 2              | 51.8             | 2                | 52.94            |
| 3              | 52.94            | 3                | 52.94            |
| 4              | 52.94            | 4                | 52.94            |
| 5              | 52.94            | 5                | 52.94            |

| 8              | 52.94            | 8                | 52.94            |

The above analysis reveals that both the K and V caches of Transition thoughts are highly robust to aggressive quantization, substantiating our choice of 2-bit precision for T thoughts. Execution thoughts similarly tolerate 4-bit quantization with negligible accuracy loss. In contrast, the K cache for Reasoning thoughts exhibits noticeably higher sensitivity—mirroring the K/V precision asymmetry reported in QAQ—while the V cache remains relatively resilient. These findings validate the precision assignments used in ThinKV. Looking ahead, extending this analysis to incorporate outlier-handling techniques or mixed K and V precisions may further reduce accuracy loss under extreme compression regimes.

In Figure 11(b) of the manuscript, we have presented a complementary ablation examining ThinKV’s precision assignment across two different models on the AIME and LiveCodeBench benchmarks. In this experiment, we employ the original formats used in the main paper—FP8 for 8-bit, NVFP4 for 4-bit, and ternary for 2-bit—which further corroborate the robustness trends observed above.

---

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our work. For clarity, we mark responses to weakness comments with **W#** and responses to explicit questions with **Q#**. 

---

## **W1: Shouldn’t reasoning model efficiency be evaluated based on end-to-end latency and normalized to serving frameworks such as vLLM?**

We fully agree with the reviewer’s recommendation, and we revised our manuscript to adopt end-to-end latency as another evaluation metric. We have been actively working on integrating ThinKV into vLLM and conducted two complementary evaluations:
(i) a dynamic serving analysis under multi-user concurrency [2], measuring real system throughput (Reqs/s) vs. E2E User latency (s), and (ii) a static analysis with batch size 1, focusing on time-per-request (TPR) and Intelligence/Watt [1] metrics. All experiments have been conducted on a single A100-80GB GPU.

#### (i) Dynamic Serving Analysis (ThinKV achieves 38\% higher loads (Reqs/s), 27\% lower latency than R-KV.)

**Table A:** Comparison of system throughput (requests per second) and end-to-end user latency across FullKV, R-KV, and ThinKV for increasing batch sizes in vLLM.

| **Batch Size** | **FullKV Throughput (Req/s)** | **FullKV User Latency (s)** | **R-KV Throughput (Req/s)** | **R-KV User Latency (s)** | **ThinKV Throughput (Req/s)** | **ThinKV User Latency (s)** |
|----------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| 1              | 0.005                         | 195                          | 0.005                        | 188                         | 0.005                         | 184                          |
| 2              | 0.009                         | 215                          | 0.011                        | 188                         | 0.011                         | 186                          |
| 4              | 0.013                         | 301.5                        | 0.020                        | 196                         | 0.021                         | 193                          |
| 8              | 0.017                         | 480                          | 0.039                        | 204                         | 0.040                         | 202                          |
| 16             | OOM                             | OOM                            | 0.073                        | 219                         | 0.077                         | 208                          |
| 32             | OOM                             | OOM                            | 0.136                        | 236                         | 0.142                         | 226                          |
| 64             | OOM                             | OOM                            | 0.163                        | 392                         | 0.215                         | 298                          |
| 128            | OOM                             | OOM                            | 0.226                        | 566                         | 0.275                         | 465                          |
| 256            | OOM                             | OOM                            | 0.259                        | 989                         | 0.356                         | 719                          |

Motivated by the dynamic-serving analyses in [2,3], we evaluate ThinKV under multi-user concurrency. For a batch size of B, we inject B parallel requests to emulate B active users and measure the achieved real system throughput (requests/s) together with the average E2E latency experienced by each user. If the method cannot support a batch size larger than a given B without running OOM, queuing delays inflate latency without increasing system throughput [2]; we therefore focus on the performance of requests that are actively executed (please let us know if you'd like to incorporate queuing delays).

Table A summarizes our findings, all reported measurements are averaged across 3 runs with B requests randomly sampled from AIME dataset with a cache budget of 1024. We added this table as Figure 9 of Section 6.2 in the revised manuscript. FullKV cannot sustain batch size more than B=8. Under an iso-batch comparison with FullKV at B=8, ThinKV achieves up to 58\% lower latency while satisfying higher requests per second. ThinKV is able to support larger batch sizes (see Table 2 in manuscript) due to high compression of the KV cache. At B=256, under iso-batch conditions, ThinKV achieves 38\% higher loads (Reqs/s) and 27\% lower latency compared to R-KV. This demonstrates that ThinKV not only improves per-request efficiency but also scales more gracefully under heavy concurrency, making it a more robust choice for practical serving workloads.

## **W2: Ablations on operator (i.e., TBQ, TBE) design.**
In Section 6.3 (Table 4 of the revised manuscript), we originally presented ablations that individually quantify the accuracy contribution of ThinKV’s core components i.e., TBQ and TBE. Following your suggestion, we have updated Table 4 (shown as Table B below) with the throughput and latency impact of ThinKV's components while also simultaneously sweeping different token budgets for TBE (without interference from TBQ) to provide an operator-isolated assessment. We also direct the reviewer to Figure 11(b) in the revised manuscript, which ablates the effect of assigning different precisions to R, T, and E thoughts. Moreover, we now also include a detailed quantization-sensitivity analysis of keys and values across different thought types in Appendix E.9.   

**Table B:** Accuracy, throughput, and latency (iso-batch) impact of ThinKV’s components, evaluated on GPT-OSS-20B using the LiveCodeBench benchmark.
| **Method**              | **Avg. Precision / Eviction Budget** | **Accuracy** | **Batch Size**   | **Norm. Throughput**   | **Norm. Latency**  |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------|--------------|----------------|------------------------|--------------------|
| FullKV                  | –                                      | 77.8         | 8              | 1x                      | 1x                  |
| TBQ                     | 3.5                                    | 77.8         | 8              | 1.1x                    |  0.98x           |
| TBE                     | 512                                    | 62.5         | 8              | 1.78x                   |  0.36x            |
| TBE                     | 1024                                   | 76.9         | 8              | 1.48x                   |  0.38x             |
| TBE                     | 2048                                   | 77.8         | 8              | 1.27x                   | 0.44x            |
| **ThinKV (TBQ+TBE)**    | **3.8, 1024**                          | **76.4**     | **8**          |  **1.51x**                 | **0.42x**             |

From Table B, we observe that ThinKV (TBQ+TBE) delivers clear throughput and latency gains even under an iso-batch comparison, while incurring only a marginal accuracy reduction relative to FullKV. More importantly, these iso-batch results understate ThinKV’s full benefit: because the hybrid compression (TBQ+TBE) substantially compresses the KV cache footprint (requiring <3.67\% of FullKV memory), ThinKV can sustain much larger batch sizes than the baseline, leading to substantial end-to-end performance improvements as shown in Table 2 in the revised manuscript.

We have also updated our manuscript with these results in Appendix E.12. 

**Table C:** Throughput (tokens/sec) evaluation of R1-Distill-Llama-8B during continuous 32K-token generation on an A100-80GB GPU, comparing FullKV, R-KV (ovl), and ThinKV integrated into vLLM.

| **Method**      | **Batch Size** | **Budget** | **Throughput ** |

Furthermore, in Figure 9 we present system throughput (reqs/sec) vs. e2e user latency (sec), also evaluated within the vLLM framework.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for taking the time to provide such a thoughtful and encouraging evaluation of our work. We greatly appreciate the recognition of our writing and presentation, contributions and strong empirical results. We address the reviewer’s questions and concerns in detail below. For clarity, we mark responses to weakness comments with **W#** and responses to explicit questions with **Q#**.

## **W1: How much acceleration can be achieved when the accuracy drop is limited to within 1\%?**

We appreciate the reviewer’s question. In the paper, we primarily report performance results (Table 2) with a 1024-token budget and R4E4T2 precision assignment (default) because this setting satisfies the ≤1\% accuracy drop criterion for the majority of evaluated LRMs and datasets (e.g., R1-Llama-8B, R1-Llama-70B on AIME and MATH-500).

**However**, we observed that a small subset of models—particularly GPT-OSS-20B on AIME and LiveCodeBench—can exhibit an accuracy drop slightly above 1\% at this setting. To provide a more conservative, accuracy-preserving configuration, we additionally report results with a 2048-token budget combined with R4E4T2 quantization. Under this configuration, all evaluated models on all datasets consistently remain within a <1\% accuracy drop, while still benefiting from ThinKV’s high compression and throughput. We summarize these results in Table A below and have incorporated it as Table 3 in Section 6.2 in the revised manuscript.

**Table A:** ThinKV throughput (tokens/s) for R1-Llama-8B on an A100-80GB GPU using a 2048-token budget performing continuous generation of 32K tokens on AIME prompts. Batch size reflects the maximum achievable value before OOM.
| **Method** | **Accuracy** | **Batch Size (max)** | **Token Budget** | **Throughput** |
|------------|--------------|-----------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| FullKV     | 50           | 13                    | –                 | 297.5           |
| **ThinKV** | 50           | **290**               | **2048**          | **4688.4**      |

Evident from Table A above, ThinKV, while sustaining a ≤1\% accuracy drop relative to FullKV, enables a drastic increase in usable batch size (13 → 290) and delivers a 15.8× throughput improvement. This demonstrates that even under conservative, accuracy-preserving settings, ThinKV enables substantial system-level acceleration without compromising model quality.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for taking the time to provide a constructive evaluation of our work. We greatly appreciate the recognition of our strong empirical results. We address the reviewer’s questions and concerns in detail below. For clarity, we mark responses to weakness comments with **W#** and responses to explicit questions with **Q#**.

---

## **W1: ThinKV is pragmatically motivated and is not based on strong theoretical and quantitative analysis.**

We appreciate the reviewer’s perspective and have revised the manuscript to explicitly clarify the underlying principles in Section 3. Specifically, ThinKV is the first to identify and leverage the *degree of attention sparsity* to systematically differentiate thought types. This decomposition arises from quantitative analysis of layer-wise attention sparsity trajectories across thousands of decoded reasoning traces (Section 3.1; Figure 3), and is formalized in Definition 1 of the manuscript. To further validate this categorization, we associate interpretable, representative keywords for each thought segment (Appendix D.2), demonstrating consistency between the sparsity-driven decomposition and distinct semantic behaviors observed in LRMs. This principled thought-type differentiation motivates ThinKV’s hybrid quantization–eviction strategy and distinguishes it from prior token-level heuristics.

Section 2 analytically characterizes how different forms of compression affect the KV-cache footprint and demonstrates empirically (Fig. 2) why quantization-only or eviction-only strategies cannot maintain a stable compression–accuracy trade-off. This motivates the unified hybrid method introduced in ThinKV. The hyperparameters (design choices) involved are a direct instantiation of this analysis and are examined through extensive ablations in Section 6.3, where we show that each contributes meaningfully to the overall behavior.

Finally, the Continuous Thinking kernel (Section 5.2) follows from a formal analysis of gather overhead—a previously overlooked bottleneck in decode-time KV eviction—and is included to ensure end-to-end system efficiency.

---

## **W2: Update figures and captions.**

Thank you for catching this typo — we have corrected Figure 1(c) in the revised manuscript. We have also updated all figure captions to be more descriptive and improve readability.

---

## **Q1: The clear separation of the three classes is very impressive in Fig 3, and Fig 14 provides other examples, for different models, but how does it hold on other datasets ?**

Thank you for recognizing the strengths of our attention-sparsity guided thought separation. Figure 14 includes examples from other datasets, including LiveCodeBench. In the revised manuscript, we have updated Figure 3 to present samples from two datasets and two models to better illustrate the generality of the three-class separation. We have also added explicit dataset labels to all plots in Figure 14 to make this correspondence clear.

---

## **Q2: How are the hyperparameters chosen ?**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. We emphasize that **ThinKV does not require per-model or per-dataset tuning**; a single well-chosen configuration works robustly across all evaluated models and benchmarks. The hyperparameters in Sections 4.1–4.3 (revised) are design choices based on empirically grounded ablation process.

For **thought decomposition** (Section 4.1), the number of thought types \(|T|\), refresh interval \(\tau\), and optimal layer subset \(|L^*|\) are ablated in Fig. 11(a) and Fig. 10(c) and discussed in Section 6.3.

For **TBQ** (Section 4.2), the quantization group size \(g = 16\) follows established practice (Alvarez et al., 2025; NVFP4). We adopt 2/4/8-bit levels because they are hardware-aligned and enable mapping precision to thought importance; this mapping is validated in Fig. 11(b) and analyzed in Section 6.3. Appendix E.8 further confirms that NVFP4, FP8, and ternary formats provide the most effective trade-offs. Furthermore, we also conducted a quantization sensitivity analysis in Appendix E.9 and find this to further validate the precision assignments used in ThinKV.

For **TBE** (Section 4.3), the retention schedule \(R = \{64, 32, 16, 8, 4\}\) and minimum retention of 4 tokens were selected based on ablations (Fig. 10a). We use powers-of-two retention to ensure memory alignment, following RocketKV (Behnam et al., 2025) and MicroScopiQ (Ramachandran et al., 2025). The progressive annealing (Fig. 10(b)) schedule preserves essential contextual traces and avoids abrupt loss of reasoning continuity.

Overall, these design choices **directly operationalize our motivating analysis** and are thoroughly ablated in Section 6.3 and Appendix E.
 
---

## **Q1: What if future reasoning model reasons in hidden states instead of explicitly outputting tokens?**

We clarify that our method does not depend on the model explicitly emitting tokens to distinguish thought types. In contrast to prior work that infers thought structure from surface-form tokens [1], ThinKV is built on a principled, sparsity-driven formulation. Thought types are differentiated through attention sparsity patterns, derived from quantitative analysis of layer-wise sparsity trajectories across thousands of traces.

Moreover, our formulation does not assume the existence of exactly three thought categories. As discussed in Sections 3.1 and 4.1, the cardinality ∣T∣ is a design choice that enables the algorithm to identify the number of thought types best supported by the underlying sparsity structure. Through ablations shown in Figure 11(a) and Section 6.3, we consistently found ∣T∣ = 3 to be optimal for all evaluated models. As long as future models continue to rely on attention-based architectures—which currently remain the most effective and widely adopted paradigm—ThinKV remains directly applicable.

In a theoretical setting where future models depart from attention-based architectures, ThinKV could still be adapted by incorporating steering vectors [1,2]. Steering vectors operate directly in the latent space and, with sufficient exploration, may offer an effective alternative to attention-sparsity–based thought differentiation if such a mechanism becomes necessary. 

[1] Venhoff, Constantin, et al. "Understanding reasoning in thinking language models via steering vectors." arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.18167 (2025).

[2] Huang, Yao, et al. "Mitigating Overthinking in Large Reasoning Models via Manifold Steering." arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.22411 (2025).

---

## **Q2: How many times of averaged score do you use for one reasoning question?**

Thank you for the question. We follow the evaluation protocol used in R-KV and adopt **pass@1** as our accuracy metric. For each question, we generate **8 independent responses** and compute pass@1 as $\text{pass@1} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} p_i$, where $p_i$ denotes whether the $i$-th sampled response is correct. Similarly for all performance measurements, throughput and latency numbers are obtained by averaging across 3 independent runs. We have updated Section 6.1 of the revised manuscript to reflect this.

---

## **Q3: Can you explain more on block size in Fig 10e (revised)?**

In ThinKV and vLLM, block\_size refers to the number of consecutive KV-cache tokens that are grouped and stored together as a single memory block within the paged KV-cache. vLLM’s PagedAttention organizes the KV cache of each sequence into fixed-size blocks of size block\_size to enable efficient non-contiguous memory allocation and reuse, and ThinKV builds directly on this design (see Figure 6, where A,B, C and D are tokens within a block of block\_size=4). The choice of block size can have a substantial impact on the performance [1]. If the block size is too small, ThinKV integrated into vLLM may not fully utilize the GPU’s parallelism for reading and processing KV cache. If the block size is too large, internal fragmentation increases, and each block may pack more thought segments per block, incurring substantial metadata overhead in the block table and increasing eviction time, which degrades performance.

Figure 10(e) presents our ablation over different ThinKV block sizes to determine the optimal configuration. From this analysis, block sizes of 8 and 16 tokens offer the strongest performance. We adopt a block size of 8 tokens, as it minimizes metadata overhead—fewer thought segments are forced into the same block. Notably, this choice aligns directly with vLLM’s own block-size analysis (Figure 18(b) in [1]).

[1] Kwon, W., Li, Z., Zhuang, S., Sheng, Y., Zheng, L., Yu, C. H., ... \& Stoica, I. (2023, October). Efficient memory management for large language model serving with pagedattention. In Proceedings of the 29th symposium on operating systems principles (pp. 611-626).

---

We hope our clarifications resolve any apprehensions and contribute to an even more favorable assessment of our work, and we would be glad to address any follow-up questions the reviewer may have.

---

## **Q2: Including additional KV cache compression methods beyond H2O and RKV in the experiments**

We would like to humbly clarify that our evaluations include a broad set of recent and state-of-the-art KV-cache compression baselines spanning both quantization and eviction approaches as described in Section 6.1. For eviction methods, we evaluate LazyEviction and RaaS in addition to H2O and R-KV, as shown in Figure 1 and 8. For quantization methods, we include KIVI and PM-KVQ, as summarized in Table 1. Across all these baselines, ThinKV consistently demonstrates superior accuracy under diverse compression ratios. For throughput evaluations, we focus primarily on R-KV because it is the closest state-of-the-art baseline to ThinKV in terms of accuracy, and it shares the gather-based eviction mechanism employed by many recent methods, including LazyEviction and RaaS. As such, R-KV serves as a strong and representative baseline for system-level comparison.

---

We hope our clarifications resolve any apprehensions and contribute to an even more favorable assessment of our work, and we would be glad to address any follow-up questions the reviewer may have.

## **Q3: What are the SoTA methods overall and what about MLA and YOCO ?**

Thank you for this valuable question. In the setting of training-free, decode-time KV-cache compression, current state-of-the-art methods fall into two main categories: eviction-based and quantization-based approaches. For eviction, R-KV (NeurIPS 2025) is the strongest published baseline, with LazyEviction and RaaS as the next most competitive methods. For quantization, PM-KVQ currently provides the strongest results. ThinKV is evaluated against all of these representative SoTA baselines in our experiments.

MLA and YOCO introduce fundamentally new model architectures, placing them outside the regime of training-free, plug-in KV-cache compression methods such as ThinKV. For this reason, direct comparison is not strictly fair, though ThinKV can in principle be integrated with any model architecture, including MLA-style designs. We note that MLA models are not yet widely available and we designate it as important future work. Consistent with prior work, our evaluations therefore use the R1-distilled models alongside several other model families.

---

## **Q4: What is the Pareto front of accuracy v/s memory footprint across methods ?**

Thank you for suggesting this. We now include an Accuracy vs. KV cache size plot in Appendix E.11, comparing ThinKV against SoTA baselines across varying eviction budgets and KV-cache precisions. We conclusively demonstrate that ThinKV sets a new Pareto-frontier. 

---

We hope our clarifications resolve any apprehensions and contribute to an even more favorable assessment of our work, and we would be glad to address any follow-up questions the reviewer may have.

Thanks for the detailed rebuttal. It resolves all my previous concerns. I just have a minor question that whether the evicted KV cache can somewhat be retrieved back in the future or it's lost forever.

summary.value:
This paper presents a combination of strategies to reduce the KV cache size during inference with a decoder transformer.

The method combines quantization and deletion of blocks of tokens in the KV cache based on a category which is inferred from the attention sparsity. The authors also propose an efficient implementation derived from PageAttention.

The resulting gain in speed for a given accuracy level beats existing methods.

strengths.value: The problem addressed by the authors is key in the deployment of large language models, and more generally reducing memory footprint is a central issue: Lower memory means possibly larger batches, larger model dimension, longer contexts, and longer / more c-o-t, which ultimately translate into smarter models.

weaknesses.value:
This is an highly engineering paper. The method proposed does not derive from a new principle nor rely on formal results or quantitative analysis. There are some motivating experiments that are interesting, but the bulk of the method is a recipe with lot of hyperparameters.

For the presentation, I encourage the authors to change the scaling of fig 1 and have both axes starting from 0, the current framing is IMO misleading. 

I am doubtful the inclusions of figures respect ICLR's style, and captions could be more detailed (e.g. fig 3, what data set?)

questions.value:
Some questions, in no specific order:

- The clear separation of the three classes is very impressive in Fig 3, and Fig 13 provides other examples, for different models, but how does it hold on other datasets? Are all this graphs from AIME?

- There are many hyperparameters in 3.2 and 3.3, how were they chosen?

- The method is compared to other KV cache quantization or eviction, but what are the sota methods overall? What about other types of methods (MLA, YOCO)? It would be great to give a clearer sense of the pareto front accuracy vs. memory footprint across methods.

Table B reports the average end-to-end request latency (Time-per-Request, TPR), accuracy, and Intelligence/Watt [1] for various KV-compression strategies evaluated on the AIME benchmark using R1-Llama-8B. ThinKV at a token budget of 1024, while simultaneously achieving lossless compression, is able to achieve up to 6\% lower latency on average per request as compared to the FullKV baseline. These gains extend beyond what a highly optimized framework like vLLM already provides, and ThinKV’s benefits become especially pronounced at larger batch sizes (refer Table A).

Recent works have demonstrated that Intelligence/Watt [1]  offers a unified view of both capability and efficiency, making it a principled metric for comparing compression strategies. As shown in Table B, these latency improvements materially increase ThinKV’s Intelligence/Watt over FullKV and R-KV. We have updated the revised manuscript with this information in Appendix E.15.


#### Clarifications on Generation Length 

We have revised Fig. 10(d) in the paper to include the impact of TBE and ThinKV (TBQ+TBE) on the generation length. On tasks such as LiveCodeBench, ThinKV increases generation length by 1.28×, and this overhead is outweighed by the benefits of KV-cache compression—namely reduced attention computation, lower memory footprint (5\% of the FullKV), and the ability to support substantially higher batch sizes (up to 54x).

[1] Saad-Falcon, J., Narayan, A., Akengin, H. O., Griffin, J., Shandilya, H., Lafuente, A. G., ... & Ré, C. (2025). Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI. arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.07885.

[2] Yu, G. I., Jeong, J. S., Kim, G. W., Kim, S., Chun, B. G. (2022). Orca: A distributed serving system for {Transformer-Based} generative models. In 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22) (pp. 521-538).

[3] Rehg, Isaac. "Kv-compress: Paged kv-cache compression with variable compression rates per attention head." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.00161 (2024).

---

## **W2: Suggestion to improve paper writing and restructure to separate motivation and methodology section.**

In the revised manuscript, we have restructured the motivation and methodology sections to create a clearer separation between the empirical observations that motivate ThinKV and the algorithmic design that follows from them.

---

## **W1: Fine-grained latency breakdown**

Thank you for highlighting the importance of detailed latency analysis. Please see Fig. 1(c) for TPOT comparison of different methods. Table 5 in the main manuscript provides a per-operation time breakdown for ThinKV at batch size 1. Crucially, Table 5 also reports the percentage of decode steps that actually invoke thought refresh or eviction, showing that ThinKV’s proactive, coarse-grained eviction strategy (Fig. 10(b)) and periodic thought refresh allow it to operate overhead-free on more than 95\% of decode steps. This is in stark contrast to R-KV, its eviction and gather operations emerge as a major bottleneck (32.91\%) since it is invoked in nearly every decoding step. 

To further address your suggestion, we extend this analysis to varying batch sizes (8 and 32) and measure the relative time contribution of key operations (Attention, MLP, TBE Eviction, and Thought Refresh). For this analysis, we focus on a representative decode step that includes all mechanisms in action. Nevertheless, the rate of calls as presented in Table 4 remain largely identical across batch sizes. We present this analysis as a figure in Appendix E.14 of the revised manuscript. Our measurements show that ThinKV’s overhead (TBE eviction + thought refresh) remains minimal across batch sizes, consistently accounting for only ~14\% of the total latency, while Attention and MLP operations dominate with more than 80–85\% of the runtime. As batch size increases, the proportion of time spent in core model execution (attention, MLP) grows, confirming that ThinKV scales efficiently with increasing batch size.


---

## **W2: Extension to long input-context workloads**

As noted in line 372 of the manuscript, we treat prefill tokens as R-type thoughts, i.e., they follow the same 4-bit precision assignment as decode-time R tokens. However, we do not evict from the prefill segment. This is because the observations in Section 3.3 applies specifically to decode-stage tokens, where attention sparsity and associations between thought types emerge naturally as the CoT unfolds. In contrast, prefill tokens constitute the entire grounding context for the task, and decode tokens continue to periodically attend back to them throughout the CoT. Evicting prefill tokens would therefore violate the core principle underlying TBE—namely, that eviction should target tokens of thought types with diminishing future attention utility. 

Applying a TBE-style eviction policy in addition to TBQ (ThinKV=TBQ+TBE) to prefill tokens requires further study. We note this limitation in Appendix F and leave it as future work. **Nonetheless, applying TBQ alone to prefill tokens still yields a 4× compression of the prefill KV cache, ensuring meaningful memory savings even without eviction**.

ThinKV, however, is orthogonal to other prefill-optimization techniques, and can be combined with them seamlessly. To illustrate this, we additionally evaluate ThinKV integrated with SnapKV on LongBench v2 [1]. LongBench v2 is a suite of long-context evaluation tasks characterized by both large input contexts and substantial output lengths. For this study, we evaluate on R1-LLama-8B and select the Code Repo QA (along the lines of SWE-Bench) task from LongBench v2, which features 16K–32K average input lengths and output sequences up to 8K tokens, making it a representative long-input/long-output setting. Prefill tokens are quantized to 4 bits using TBQ and evicted according to SnapKV’s eviction policy under varying budgets, while the decode stage employs ThinKV with a fixed KV-cache budget of 512 tokens. Our results are summarized in Table E below.

**Table E:** Ablation of Prefill and Decode Settings for Hybrid (SnapKV +ThinKV) Compression

| **Method**        | **Prefill Precision/Eviction Budget** | **Decode Precision/Eviction Budget** | **Accuracy** |
|-------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|--------------|
| FullKV            | –                        | –                        | 30           |
| ThinKV            | 4-bits                   | 3.8/512                 | 28           |
| SnapKV + ThinKV   | 4-bits/2048              | 3.7/512                 | 24           |
| SnapKV + ThinKV   | 4-bits/4096             | 3.8/512                 | 28           |

Evidently, ThinKV incurs only a small accuracy drop, despite achieving 4x prefill compression and up to 66x decode compression. When combined with SnapKV, accuracy depends largely on the prefill eviction budget: 2048-token budget reduces accuracy by 6\%, while a 4096-token budget yields only a modest accuracy degradation. 

---

We hope our clarifications resolve any apprehensions and contribute to an even more favorable assessment of our work, and we would be glad to address any follow-up questions the reviewer may have.

summary.value: This paper introduces a novel approach to KV Cache management specifically designed for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). Recognizing that these models generate extremely long sequences, leading to significant KV Cache demands, the authors address that existing methods often overlook the unique characteristics of reasoning models. The core contribution lies on observations about attention sparsity variations across different reasoning stages. Based on these findings, the proposed method, ThinKV, dynamically manages the KV Cache through a combination of quantization and eviction strategies. This approach aims to simultaneously reduce latency and improve peak throughput, enhancing the overall efficiency of LRM inference.

strengths.value:
* **A Novel Design.** The paper introduces a thought-adaptive framework that maps attention sparsity to reasoning stages, enabling hybrid mixed-precision quantization and adaptive eviction. This design achieves fine-grained, semantically informed KV cache compression beyond traditional token-level compressions.
* **A Comprehensive Implementation.** ThinKV is supported by a strong system-level realization, featuring gather-free memory reuse via an extension from vLLM mechanism and fused dequantization–matrix multiplication inspired by KiVi. The paper further provides detailed kernel-level breakdowns and overhead analyses, demonstrating solid engineering rigor.
* **A Strong Result.** Across math and coding benchmarks, ThinKV consistently achieves higher accuracy under different memory budgets and higher throughput compared to R-KV, showcasing both algorithmic and system-level efficiency gains.

weaknesses.value:
* **Lack of Latency Comparison.** Although Section 5 reports throughput under large-batch settings, the paper does not present a detailed latency analysis. For large reasoning models (LRMs), metrics especially TPOT (Time per Output Token) are critical, as generated sequence will be long and interactive responsiveness matters. A fine-grained latency breakdown across decoding steps or batch sizes would strengthen the system-level evaluation.
* **Limited on long input tasks.** ThinKV is evaluated on datasets whose input prompts average only a few hundred tokens. However, some practical workloads (e.g., SWE-bench [1]) involve very long input contexts. Since ThinKV does not compress the prefill cache, its effectiveness and efficiency under long-input regimes remain unclear.



[1] Jimenez, Carlos E., et al. "SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-world Github Issues?." ICLR. 2024.

questions.value:
* **Accuracy–Efficiency Trade-off with Non-Reasoning Modes.**
   While ThinKV improves accuracy relative to other compression baselines, it still introduces slight degradation compared to Full Cache. Recent models such as the Qwen3 series support *optional reasoning (thinking vs. direct answer)* modes. It would be valuable to compare ThinKV-enabled reasoning against no-thinking (full attention) decoding, to quantify whether the added reasoning—and compression—yields net gains in both accuracy and efficiency.
* **Sensitivity of different Thought Types to Quantization Precision.**
   Section 3.2.2 discusses precision settings on different reasoning stages. Prior work such as QAQ [2] demonstrates that Key and Value Cache have different sensitivity on precision. A similar quantization-sensitivity study across thought types would clarify the boundary of compression on different reasoning stages.

[2] Dong, Shichen, et al. "Qaq: Quality adaptive quantization for llm kv cache." arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.04643 (2024).

**Answer to follow-up question:** Consistent with prior work on KV cache compression for LLMs and LRMs, evicted KV entries are discarded and cannot be retrieved (the token-dropping paradigm). However, as our experiments in Figure 10(a) demonstrate, ThinKV sustains recall rates close to FullKV across a wide range of token budgets. Recall rate measures the fraction of important tokens (Top-10) preserved by a compression method relative to those under full attention at each decoding step. Consequently, ThinKV’s thought-adaptive eviction scheme obfuscates the need to retrieve evicted tokens, as it consistently retains the optimal subset of high-impact tokens. This behavior is further corroborated by our near-lossless performance across models and datasets even at a 1024-token KV budget.

That said, should retrieval of evicted tokens ever be required, the techniques proposed in ThinKV are orthogonal to the token offloading and retrieval literature [1,2]. Along these lines, after ThinKV’s TBE stage, evicted tokens could be offloaded to CPU memory and later retrieved for subsequent decoding steps. **We would be happy to conduct such an experiment if the reviewer finds it valuable**.
